title: What I Think of The Results of the U.S. Midterm Elections
snippet: Many people have asked what I think of the results of the U.S.
content_html:
Many people have asked what I think of the results of the U.S. midterm elections, so I decided to pass along my thoughts in writing. Because there are too many implications of the changes in the various seats of government to cover in this brief note, I will just focus on the most important ones.

My big picture conclusion is that these political changes won’t change the circumstances that our representatives in government have to deal with. Our problems won’t go away and what matters above all else is whether the representatives deal with them in an effective bipartisan way or an ineffective confrontational way. More specifically, we will have the same debt issues, the same wealth and values gap issues, the same international geopolitical issues, the same climate issues, and the same technology issues, and the election results won’t change the dynamics of how things such as fights over wealth and power typically work. The midterm elections will just change who will be dealing with these issues and how.

The most important question is whether there will be more fighting and dysfunction or less; I think it is likely there will be more fighting and more dysfunction.

We will soon see whether I am right or wrong, starting with how the lame-duck session goes and what happens after it, which will affect many issues. For example, we will see how the chosen government representatives deal with the subject of money, more specifically the government’s spending and taxing of it. That issue will resurface on December 11 when President Trump’s temporary funding expires, then again in March 2027 when the Federal debt is projected to hit its limit, and again in the fall of 2027 when the Treasury is projected to run out of funds options. It is likely that the fights over these funding issues will be brutal and that the fighting and uncertainty will probably raise Treasury bill and similar short-term yields because investors will want to avoid payment uncertainty. It is also likely that there will be increasing worries about liquidity and credit risks, which will undermine confidence in Treasury securities as the world’s principal safe collateral. Similarly, it is likely that Elizabeth Warren being head of the Senate Banking Committee will lead to fights and changes that will affect the economy and markets.

These are just a few examples of the many such disruptions that will happen.

The election changes will also leave the U.S. with a wounded, lame-duck president under attack in a kind of civil war (probably peaceful) with an isolationist population and isolationist opposition and facing a big debt/money problem. That will weaken him and the U.S. internationally and will likely lead to U.S. retrenchment, which will lead to increased influence of the countries with the greatest powers in each major geographic region (for example, China in Asia).

As for what’s needed, I still believe that, as a principle, * there is only one possible successful path forward for the United States and all other over-indebted, financially/socially/ politically fractured democracies that are suffering from the same problems (e.g., France, other European nations, and the UK), and that is to have smart and strong moderates of the left and the right work together against the extremists to deal well with the difficult issues, which will require them to agree and get the government and the people of the country to do the difficult things that will make them strong again. I also still think that is very unlikely.

As for the politics, we have seen this internal political dynamic happen throughout history because there have always been political disagreements and at least four different political perspectives about what to do about them, which, on a continuum from left to right, consist of 1) the extreme left, 2) the moderate left, 3) the moderate right, and 4) the extreme right. As conditions get worse, these groups become increasingly polarized so that those on the left and those on the right increasingly fight against those on the opposite side until one side (the left or the right) wins, at which point the moderates and the extremists on the winning side fight each other for control. This fighting has always increased for the logical reason that when wealth and values gaps increase, irreconcilable differences become greater. We are now seeing these sorts of fights emerging in both the Republican and Democratic parties. I expect to see a lot more of both intra- and inter- party fighting.

In my opinion, this political dynamic is due to how human nature works. It has happened everywhere throughout history, and it is happening now in almost every country, with some slight differences. For example, in China, which is hierarchical because of the culture (primarily Confucian), there is always a strong hierarchy; however, the degrees of this hierarchy swing between extremely hierarchical and more open to debate. Right now in the U.S., this is what has been going on with the extreme parts of each party demanding control, so there has been a near-violent fight between the two parties that is now morphing into a fight within each party. In many other countries, this would have led to the creation of more than two parties. However, given that the two existing parties have much greater resources than any potential startup party, breaking into more parties is widely considered impractical.

Regarding the issues that the parties are fighting over, I have been like a broken record on this for so long that I presume that you know my thinking about there being Five Big Forces that typically transpire in a Big Cycle, about how these forces have been transpiring this time, and about where we are in the Big Cycle. For that reason, I won’t get into them again. Besides, I believe that you know what is healthy and unhealthy because it is basic and obvious, so I presume that you can tell whether what is happening now is healthy or unhealthy. I also believe that you can understand what is required to make the U.S. financially strong again because it isn’t complicated and because it has always been true. For example, the financial laws of nature concerning borrowing money are the same for governments as they are for people (e.g., you can’t constantly spend more than you make without consequences), except that governments can print money to make debts easier to pay, which devalues the debt. These truths have been clear for thousands of years. So, we should know where the U.S. stands and understand that there is no getting around the need for those in government to do the painful, healthy things that are required to make the U.S. productively and financially strong again. And that doesn’t look likely to happen because the people who vote don’t want to do the hard things to get the country’s finances in order—e.g., they don’t want the raising of taxes and/or the cutting benefits and they can’t agree on how to deal with the debt. This will come to a head soon.

As a person who believes that the only way to have a successful path forward is by having smart moderates from both sides work well together, I do think that it’s noteworthy and very important that most of the Democrats who got elected in the swing states appeared almost indistinguishable from moderate Republicans, so to call them “Democrats” and to describe the split as between Democrats and Republicans is overly simplistic. Most of the Democrats who got elected in previously “red” states look nothing like the hard left Democrats (e.g., the Democratic Socialists of America) even though they also go by the name of Democrats. It’s also worth noting that the democratic norms of voting and accepting election results held across the country. While it was a big win for democracy, the big question of whether democracy can be effective remains.

In 2021, my book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order came out, and it predicted what has happened since then by describing the Big Cycle and the cause-effect relationships that drive it through its six stages. In the book, I describe the late part of the Big Cycle with a special focus on Stage 5 and Stage 6 of the domestic cycle that swings between order and disorder. It’s on pages 167-191 of the book, or you can find it in this article I shared last year.

As Winston Churchill said in 1948, “those who fail to learn from history are condemned to repeat it.”

Since I have already gone on too long, I decided to wait a couple of days to pass along what I believe the Democrats, or the Republicans, or them working together need to deliver in order to win in the future. If they can keep this single most important thing top of mind, agree that they need it, understand what produces it, and then work on delivering it, everything will be a lot better. I’ll explain it in my next note.
